clue.text: Stop working on TV? One may suddenly appear in play

definitions.text: One may suddenly appear in play

blocks.note: to jack in a job is British slang for giving it up
the box is a colloquial name for television, so being on TV is being on the box

explanation.surface: Someone retires from television, and a new face may suddenly turn up in a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack in' is British slang for quit. 'Play' here means a child's playtime, not theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The toy is a box from which a sprung figure leaps out without warning when a child plays with it.

clue.text: Aircraft landing straight down in clear stream

blocks.note: to clear a fence is to leap over it
a jet is a stream of liquid or gas

explanation.surface: A plane comes down vertically into a clear-running brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like an adjective for the stream, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A Harrier-type plane takes off and lands vertically, which is what landing straight down describes.

clue.text: Somerset's ale made a novel combination with this food

definitions.text: Somerset's ale made a novel combination with this food

blocks.clueFragment: Somerset's ale made a novel combination with this food
blocks.note: surface reading: a West Country beer paired with some dish

blocks.clueFragment: Somerset's ale made a novel combination
blocks.note: setter's reading: Somerset Maugham wrote a novel whose title joins ale with a food

explanation.surface: A cider-country beer is paired with an unusual food.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is the English county but also the novelist W. Somerset Maugham, whose 1930 novel is called Cakes and Ale.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing food in the Maugham title pairs with ale, giving the baked treats that complete it.

clue.text: Prompt in way I punish

blocks.note: taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written
to gate a pupil is to confine them to school as punishment

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to be on time in their punishments.
explanation.walkthrough: Gating is British school and university slang for confining someone to the premises.
explanation.definitionFit: To instigate something is to bring it about or urge it on, as a prompt does.

clue.text: Administer punishment that's corporal

blocks.note: surface reading: a sergeant-major type handing out punishment
setter's reading: physical punishment, a beating or thrashing

explanation.surface: Discipline is handed out, perhaps by an army NCO.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporal looks like the army rank, but corporal punishment is a beating. Trim is an old informal verb for thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: In dated slang, to trim someone meant to give them a thrashing, a physical chastisement.

clue.text: Catch fish with special net initially

indicators.note: special suggests a version made out of the ordinary, so the word's letters are rearranged
initially says this part comes first, before the other piece is joined on

blocks.note: the three letters to rearrange
to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: An angler lands a fish using a purpose-made net.
explanation.walkthrough: The fishing clue word is a verb here, giving the second part, and the scrambled net goes in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To entangle is to snare or trap something so that it cannot get free, as a net does.

clue.text: Italian town that's old? It's a ruin

indicators.note: to ruin a thing is to wreck it, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
the four letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An ancient Italian place lies in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin' looks like a noun for the old town, but it is the command to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostia was the ancient harbour town of Rome at the Tiber mouth, now an excavated site and modern resort.

clue.text: Author appearing in West End hall

indicators.note: appearing in says the name shows up inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A writer makes a personal appearance at a London theatre venue.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre district.
explanation.definitionFit: Stendhal was the pen name of the French novelist who wrote Le Rouge et le Noir.

clue.text: Recovered with maiden over

blocks.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
finished

explanation.surface: A cricketer gets back to form after bowling a maiden over.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a maiden is an over with no runs conceded. 'Maiden over' looks like one phrase, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has mended has got better after illness or injury, just as a recovered patient has.

clue.text: Force to change gear in emergency

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: describing something used in an emergency

blocks.note: to make someone do something is to force them
in American usage you shift gears when driving

explanation.surface: A driver is compelled to change gear suddenly during some crisis on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Something makeshift is a temporary stopgap improvised when nothing better is available, as happens in a crisis.

clue.text: Union support for driver who's a learner?

blocks.note: TU is the abbreviation for trade union
in golf a driver is a club, and the ball sits on a tee before it is struck

explanation.surface: Seems to ask about union backing for a learner driver, a motorist on L-plates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' suggests a car, but it is the golf club that the tee supports.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutee is a pupil receiving tuition from a tutor, hence someone being taught.

clue.text: In France, I become religious member of society

blocks.note: je is French for I
a colour that becomes you suits you

explanation.surface: A French speaker announces joining a religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jesuits are the Society of Jesus, so 'society' here is a capital-S name in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesuits are priests and brothers of the Society of Jesus, the Catholic order founded by Ignatius Loyola.

clue.text: Daunted, is automatically running

blocks.note: first meaning: deprived of courage, unnerved
second meaning: operating with no crew aboard

explanation.surface: Someone is intimidated and flees on reflex.
explanation.definitionFit: To be unmanned is to lose one's nerve; an unmanned craft or station operates without any human crew.

clue.text: Vessel with sails of striped material

blocks.note: first meaning: a small single-masted Mediterranean boat
second meaning: woollen cloth woven in crossing coloured bands

explanation.surface: A boat whose canvas is made of patterned cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The boat sense is rare: a tartan, or tartane, is a lateen-rigged coasting vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish plaid cloth has bands of colour crossing each other, and a tartane is an old Mediterranean coasting craft.

clue.text: Interpret sound in tune even better

blocks.note: to read a situation is to interpret it
a sound argument is valid or fair

explanation.surface: Musicians are asked to make sense of a noise and sing more accurately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' and 'tune' suggest music; sound here means fair or valid.
explanation.definitionFit: To readjust is to alter settings again, refining them further as one fine-tunes an instrument or engine.

clue.text: Careless with old ships at sea

indicators.note: being at sea is being confused and disoriented, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A navy is criticised for negligence in keeping antiquated vessels afloat.
explanation.definitionFit: Slipshod work is sloppy and done without due attention, like shoes worn down at the heel.

clue.text: Sort of magazine chosen by college, say

indicators.note: say means speak the words out, so they are judged by how they sound

blocks.note: selected
Oriel is a college of Oxford University

explanation.surface: A magazine is selected by a university college, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example', but it signals a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A pictorial is a magazine that relies chiefly on photographs and illustrations rather than text.

clue.text: What the Lady of Shalott left, including one special bequest

indicators.note: including means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.clueFragment: What the Lady of Shalott left
blocks.note: in Tennyson's poem she left the web and left the loom to look at Lancelot
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Seems to ask what the Lady of Shalott bequeathed in her will.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's line is 'She left the web, she left the loom'; 'left' looks like bequeathed, but she simply walked away from it.
explanation.definitionFit: An heirloom is a treasured item handed down through a family from one generation to the next.

clue.text: Main complaint the Poet Laureate produced

blocks.note: the main is an old word for the open ocean
an illness or ailment

explanation.surface: Seems to name the chief grievance a Poet Laureate came up with.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield, Poet Laureate 1930-67, wrote the poem beginning 'I must go down to the seas again'. 'Main' looks like an adjective but is the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Masefield's best-known poem is titled with this phrase, so it is a work the Laureate wrote.

clue.text: Fast dog coming into view

indicators.note: coming into something means entering it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: to view is to see
a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A speedy hound comes into sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speedy, describing the dog, but it means fixed firmly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made fast is fixed firmly in place and cannot come loose, which is what secure means.

clue.text: Grave stone cut by copper disc

indicators.note: a word cut by others is split open so they sit in its middle

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A gravestone is sliced through by a copper plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like a tomb or a serious adjective, but it is the verb meaning to carve.
explanation.definitionFit: To grave is an old verb for carving or engraving, which is what a sculptor does to shape stone.

clue.text: Actress, out of condition, appears to act frightfully

definitions.note: a verb phrase: to cause fright

indicators.note: read as outside of, so the actress's name wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: Ellen Terry was the great Victorian Shakespearean actress
if introduces a condition

explanation.surface: An unfit actress seems to perform dreadfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of condition' reads as unfit, but it means the actress sits outside the word for condition.
explanation.definitionFit: To terrify is to fill someone with dread, behaving in a way that causes fright.

clue.text: It's clear Joy resorted to this form of persuasion

indicators.note: re-sorted means sorted again, so the letters are put into a fresh order

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Plainly a woman called Joy fell back on coaxing to get her way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resorted' seems to mean fell back on, but split as re-sorted it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Cajolery is wheedling flattery used to coax someone into doing what you want.

clue.text: Volume provided light read? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means only half is kept, so the second half of the word is dropped

blocks.note: lit means set alight, past tense of light
taken as written

explanation.surface: A book is offered as easy holiday reading, and someone scoffs 'Not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is a British exclamation meaning very much so; here it literally halves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A litre is a metric unit of capacity, a measure of volume.

clue.text: One audibly affected by illness, in chest

indicators.note: audibly means heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its pronunciation

blocks.note: someone with a bad cold who keeps hacking

explanation.surface: A sick person's illness has settled on the lungs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In chest' reads like the site of the illness, but chest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffer is a strongbox for keeping money or valuables.

clue.text: Learner just about showing natural aptitude

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: fair and just both mean impartial
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A beginner reveals a born talent, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just about' looks like 'nearly', but just is a word in its own right, and about wraps it round the learner.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is an instinctive talent or knack for doing something well.

clue.text: A book's shortened before edit -— don't take it lying down

indicators.note: shortened means cut down, so the words lose their ends

blocks.note: taken as written
B is an abbreviation for book
taken as written

explanation.surface: An author whose book is being cut resolves to fight back rather than accept it meekly.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'don't take it lying down' means resist; only its last two words define, cheekily, the state of being in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Abed is an old word for in bed, where one normally reclines horizontally.

clue.text: Another exam one's taken during holiday

indicators.note: something taken during a period happens within it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a break from work
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A student has to retake a test in the middle of the vacation.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools and universities a resit is a second attempt at a failed exam.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is the repeat sitting of an examination, given to candidates who failed the first.

clue.text: Treat big bat with oil, for essential contributions to score

indicators.note: to treat something is to work on it, so these letters are processed into a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange; with is a joining word

explanation.surface: Oiling a cricket bat is vital for building a big score.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture hides a musical score; obbligato is the Italian plural form.
explanation.definitionFit: An obbligato is an instrumental part a composer marks as indispensable, so it must be played in performance.

clue.text: Wandering down memory lane not on for these old warriors?

indicators.note: the phrase asks for the little word on to be left out of the fodder
wandering means straying from a set path, so the letters stray from their order

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to work with

explanation.surface: Veterans reminisce about their soldiering days.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one O and one N, then rearrange the rest. The New Model Army was Parliament's force in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell's reorganised parliamentary troops of 1645 were seventeenth-century soldiers, fitting old warriors.
